reason: The Chicago Fire history project directly supports the inquiry, O’Leary testimony, and attributed later boast; the council record supports the 1997 exoneration.
story: The Great Chicago Fire began near the O’Leary barn on October 8, 1871, and left about 100,000 homeless. Catherine O’Leary testified she was asleep; the official inquiry found no proof against her. The exact cause remains unknown. Forty years later, Michael Ahern boasted that he and two others invented the cow story, though the authorship of his later account is disputed. Chicago’s council exonerated O’Leary in 1997.
angle: The cow story survived even though the 1871 inquiry found no proof against O’Leary and its supposed inventor’s later account is disputed.

claims.claim: The fire began on October 8, 1871, near the O’Leary barn.
The fire left about 100,000 Chicagoans homeless.
The cow story blamed a cow for a fire whose exact cause remains unproved.
Catherine O’Leary testified under oath that she was in bed when the fire began.
The official inquiry found no proof of Catherine O’Leary’s guilt.
Forty years later, Michael Ahern boasted that he and two others invented the cow story; authorship of his account is disputed.
Chicago City Council exonerated Catherine O’Leary in 1997.

disputed: Ahern’s later boast is documented, but another writer claimed to have ghostwritten the account, and others have been credited with originating the legend. Do not state that Ahern alone invented it as fact.
The exact cause of the 1871 fire has never been proved. Do not state that the cow could not have been involved.
